title: US Visa Processing Delays Force Indian Students to Defer University Enrollment
excerpt: FIFA World Cup visa prioritization and expanded travel bans have displaced student visa processing, with enrollment of international students projected to drop by more than 100,000 this fall.
body:
• International student enrollment in the US is projected to decline by more than 100,000 for the 2026-27 academic year due to visa processing delays and policy uncertainty.
  • The State Department's decision to prioritize FIFA World Cup ticket holder visas displaced the traditional spring-summer student visa processing window.
  • Indian students face elevated denial rates, with some receiving rejections weeks after interviews — just days before classes begin.
  • A new Duration of Status rule taking effect September 15 replaces the open-ended F-1 framework with a fixed four-year cap, adding further uncertainty.

Student Visa Processing Pushed Aside for World Cup

The US State Department's decision to prioritize visa processing for FIFA World Cup ticket holders traveling to the United States this year has displaced the historical practice of fast-tracking student visa applicants during the peak spring and summer months, according to analysis by ICEF Monitor. The shift has created widespread processing bottlenecks at consulates in India, China, and across Europe.

International applications filed through the Common App platform are down 9% for the coming academic year. The Association of American Universities Data Exchange reports that the international pool of doctoral candidates shrank by 21% for 2026-27, contributing to an overall 17% decline in international PhD admissions. Nearly two-thirds of respondents to the Institute of International Education's Spring Snapshot Survey expect enrollment declines.

"US policy and regulations affect where international students plan to invest their future — and their decisions carry significant short- and long-term consequences for US society and economy."

— Institute of International Education

Indian Students Hit Hardest

Indian students are being denied F-1 visas at rates not seen in at least five years, according to Sudhanshu Kaushik, director of the North American Association of Indian Students. Many applicants are told they have not provided sufficient proof that they do not intend to immigrate — a standard reason that has now become common even among wealthier students from major Indian cities with deep roots and connections in India.

"A demographic that's never had an issue is facing lots of issues," Kaushik told Inside Higher Ed. He noted that some students are receiving denial notifications weeks after their visa interviews, in some cases just days before their planned enrollment dates.

An expanded travel ban affecting citizens from 39 countries, including Nigeria, has been in effect since January 1, 2026. While there has not been an outright pause on visa processing this year, the combination of World Cup prioritization, expanded bans, and policy uncertainty has created a compounding effect on student mobility.

Duration of Status Rule Adds New Pressure

Compounding the processing delays is a new Duration of Status rule scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026. The regulation replaces the longstanding framework under which international students could remain in the US for the duration of their academic program with a fixed four-year cap, after which students must apply for extensions.

Legal challenges are underway. The core question before the courts is whether the Department of Homeland Security has the statutory authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act to replace the duration of status framework without explicit congressional authorization, according to analysis by LawStreet Journal.

International students contribute over $40 billion annually to the US economy through tuition, housing, and living expenses. India alone accounts for more than $10 billion of that figure. With Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia actively competing for the same pool of internationally mobile Indian students, the combined effect of processing delays and policy changes could produce a durable shift in where these students choose to study.

Universities Scramble to Accommodate

American universities are responding with a mix of deferrals, online class options, and creative workarounds. Cornell University has developed a "global semester program" offering international students who could not secure visas in time the option to spend their first semester at one of three international partner institutions before transferring to Cornell in the spring.

Other institutions are extending census deadlines and offering late-start enrollment windows. But for students who have already arranged housing, secured financing, and planned their academic trajectory, even a one-semester delay can cascade through their educational and career timelines.

What to Watch

The September 15 implementation date for the Duration of Status rule will be the next inflection point. Court challenges could delay or modify the rule, but universities and students have fewer than two weeks to adapt. Meanwhile, post-World Cup visa processing is expected to gradually return to normal capacity at Indian consulates, though the backlog may take months to clear.
